stories.title: 260 Fake Jack Ma Videos Are Tricking People About Singapore
stories.headline_kid: Someone used a computer trick to make fake videos that look like a famous businessman talking about Singapore — and over a million people have already watched them!
summary: News investigators at CNA discovered something sneaky online: 260 fake videos on YouTube that look like they show Jack Ma, the famous founder of the company Alibaba, talking about Singapore. But Jack Ma never actually said any of these things! The videos were made using AI, a kind of smart computer programme that can copy a person's face and voice to make it seem like they are really speaking.

These videos mix some nice compliments about Singapore with false information, trying to confuse people about what is true. Together, the fake videos have already been watched more than 1 million times. That is like every single pupil in every primary school in Singapore watching it more than ten times each!

CNA's investigators found something suspicious: five different YouTube channels using Jack Ma's face were all created within just five days of each other, and some posted the exact same video within seconds of one another. This pattern suggests it was planned by one group, not by accident.

This matters because spreading false stories, called disinformation, can make people trust their own country less or believe things that simply are not true. It is a reminder that not everything we see online — even videos that look very real — is actually real.

lenses.me: If you see a video online that seems surprising or too dramatic, pause and ask an adult before believing or sharing it.
lenses.family: Your family should always check if a video's source is trustworthy before believing or forwarding it in chat groups.
lenses.friends: Your classmates might see these videos too — talking about them together can help everyone spot what's fake.
lenses.nation: Singapore takes false information seriously because it can confuse citizens and hurt trust in our country.
lenses.world: This shows how AI tools can be misused anywhere in the world to spread lies that look very convincing.

stories.title: Oil Prices Drop After Two Countries Stop Fighting
stories.headline_kid: When the USA and Iran agreed to stop attacking each other, the price of oil dropped fast — and that could mean cheaper petrol and bus rides for us!
summary: The United States and Iran have been in a tense stand-off, taking turns launching strikes against each other. This week, both sides agreed to pause their attacks. As soon as this happened, the price of oil around the world dropped sharply — falling more than 8% to about US$88 for one barrel.

Oil is important because it is turned into petrol for cars, buses and planes, and is also used to make many everyday products. When countries near the Middle East, where a lot of the world's oil comes from, are fighting, people worry that oil supplies might be disrupted. This fear usually makes oil prices go up.

Now that the fighting has paused, that fear has eased a little, so prices came down. But experts warn this doesn't mean the problem is fully solved — the tension between the two countries has only calmed down, not disappeared completely.

For Singapore, which buys almost all its oil from overseas, lower oil prices could mean petrol, bus and taxi fares, and even flight tickets don't get more expensive for now. But if the fighting starts again, prices could shoot back up.

lenses.me: You might notice petrol prices at the pump (if your family drives) staying steady instead of rising.
lenses.family: Your family's transport costs, like petrol or Grab rides, could stay more affordable for a while.
lenses.friends: Bus and MRT fares are partly linked to fuel costs, so this news could affect how much your family spends getting to school.
lenses.nation: Singapore imports almost all its energy, so changes in world oil prices directly affect our cost of living.
lenses.world: This shows how conflicts in one part of the world can quickly affect prices everywhere, even far away in Singapore.

stories.title: Too Many EV Charging Shops in Singapore?
stories.headline_kid: Singapore has 36 companies racing to build electric car charging stations — but there might not be enough electric cars yet to keep them all in business!
summary: Electric vehicles, or EVs, are cars that run on batteries instead of petrol. Just like your phone needs charging, EVs need to plug into charging stations to keep running. Because Singapore wants more people to switch to EVs to help the environment, many companies rushed to build charging stations across the island.

Right now, there are 36 different EV charging companies in Singapore. That's a lot of competition! Recently, two of these companies have shut down, and one company was bought over by a bigger business, called a buyout.

Experts believe the industry may have grown too fast, building more charging points than there are electric cars to use them right now. It's a bit like opening too many bubble tea shops on the same street before enough customers show up — some shops just can't survive.

This matters because Singapore is trying to get more people driving electric cars by 2030 to cut down on pollution. If charging companies keep closing, it could slow down that plan, but if the strongest companies survive, EV charging could become easier and more reliable for everyone.

lenses.me: If your family ever gets an electric car, you'll want to know there are enough working charging stations around.
lenses.family: Families thinking about buying an EV should check how easy it is to find a reliable charging station nearby.
lenses.friends: You might notice more electric cars on the road as Singapore pushes towards cleaner transport.
lenses.nation: Singapore's plan to fight pollution depends on having enough good charging infrastructure for EVs.
lenses.world: Many countries are facing the same challenge — building enough charging stations before enough people own electric cars.

stories.title: Many Singapore Workers Feel Bored at Their Jobs
stories.headline_kid: A survey found only 14 out of 100 workers in Singapore feel truly excited about their jobs — that means many parents might be coming home feeling a bit flat.
summary: A big worldwide survey by a research company called Gallup found that only 14% of workers in Singapore felt 'engaged' at their jobs in 2025. Being engaged means feeling interested, motivated and connected to what you do — kind of like how excited you feel playing a game you truly enjoy, instead of doing homework you find boring.

This number is lower than the average around the world, and even lower than the average in Southeast Asia. It suggests many working adults in Singapore, possibly including some of your parents, may not feel very happy or excited about work.

A commentary writer from Singapore Management University says this matters because if everyone believes workers are unhappy no matter what, companies might stop trying to make workplaces better. He argues that we should not simply accept feeling disengaged — bosses and workers together should keep working to make jobs more enjoyable and meaningful.
Feeling engaged at work is important because happier workers usually do better work and feel less stressed, which can also make home life happier for their families.

lenses.me: You might notice your parents feeling tired or less cheerful after work — it's not because of you, but because of how their workday went.
lenses.family: Understanding this can help you be more patient and caring when a parent seems tired after a long work day.
lenses.friends: Your friends' parents might feel the same way, since this challenge affects many families across Singapore.
lenses.nation: A less engaged workforce could affect how well companies and Singapore's economy perform in the future.
lenses.world: Singapore's low engagement numbers reflect a challenge many countries face as work and technology change quickly.

stories.title: 59-Year-Old Footballer Scores His First Goal in Four Years!
stories.headline_kid: Meet 'King Kazu' — a Japanese footballer who is still scoring goals at age 59, proving you're never too old to chase your dreams!
summary: Kazuyoshi Miura, nicknamed 'King Kazu', is a Japanese footballer who has been playing professionally since 1986 — that's 40 years ago! At 59 years old, he recently scored his first competitive goal in almost four years, helping his team, Fukushima United, win 7-0.

Most professional footballers retire in their thirties, but King Kazu has kept playing for decades, becoming a symbol of never giving up on something you love. He signed with Fukushima United, a team in Japan's third division league, earlier this year on loan.

His story has inspired fans across Asia, including in Singapore, where many older citizens are also encouraged to stay active through programmes like the Silver Generation initiatives. It shows that age doesn't have to stop someone from doing what they enjoy, whether it's sports, art or learning something new.
King Kazu's incredible career reminds us all — young and old — that passion, patience and hard work can help us achieve amazing things at any age.

lenses.me: King Kazu's story can inspire you to keep practising something you love, even if it feels hard sometimes.
lenses.family: Grandparents or older relatives in your family might find his story encouraging to stay active as they age.
lenses.friends: You and your friends could talk about your own sports heroes and what makes them special.
lenses.nation: Singapore also promotes active ageing, encouraging seniors to stay fit and involved in activities like sports.
lenses.world: His achievement shows how passion for sport can inspire people across different countries and cultures.
